newsitem.title: USA: Inflation-indexed bonds - new vogue in corporates?.
newsitem.headline: Inflation-indexed bonds - new vogue in corporates?.

text.p: The volume of non-government agency inflation-indexed corporate bonds doubled on Thursday in what could be a rapidly developing new market, some syndicate officials said.
Issuance will be concentrated in the highest quality credits for the time being as investors get acclimated to the structure's innate features, they said.
"I think investors first want to understand the product without having to make two decisions," said John Massad, head of J.P. Morgan's debt syndicate.
"There's one decision about the product and they don't want to have to make another decision about credit," Massad said.

J.P. Morgan & Co Inc issued $200 million in 15-year Aa3/AA rated CPI-linked securities on Thursday, priced to yield four percentage points over CPI. That issue, the first from an issuer with ratings below triple-A, was increased in size by $100 million.
The firm also led a $100 million five-year CPI-linked note deal for Toyota's Toyota Motor Credit Corp. The triple-A rated issue was priced to yield 3.2 percentage points over CPI.

The Tennessee Valley Authority, a quasi-government agency, sold $300 million in CPI-linked power bonds on Wednesday. Lead underwriter Merrill Lynch & Co said it recorded about $600 in orders for the deal.
One official at Merrill Lynch, who declined to be named, said the deal was kept at its original size to ensure it traded well in the secondary market.
Federal Home Loan Bank System, a government agency, was the first to use the structure following the U.S. Treasury's blowout sale of $7.0 billion 10-year inflation indexed bonds on January 29.
Deals from lower-A-rated corporate issuers are not in the pipeline yet, syndicate officials said, but they can't be too far in the offing if the market is to grow.
"There will be an extension of rating in order to accumulate more spread," said the Merrill Lynch official.
He added "if it doesn't happen within a year, it won't happen because it will get old."
Traditional corporate buyers, including insurance companies, pension funds and money managers were actively vying for the paper, Morgan's Massad said.
A hedge against inflation may be the most obvious selling point, but Massad said the notes have also sold to buyers looking to maximize total return or to match liabilities to the CPI.

Nanette Abuhoff, J.P. Morgan's fixed-income strategist, said that "compared to Treasury issues, corporate inflation-linked notes offer higher real yields and, when issued in the current pay structure, have higher coupons."
